All graphs are finite, simple, and undirected. Cycles are considered as subgraphs, not necessarily induced subgraphs. A graph homomorphism from \(G\) to \(H\) is a map \(f:V(G)\to V(H)\) such that \(f(u)f(v)\in E(H)\) whenever \(uv\in E(G)\); the map need not be injective.

For a real number \(c\in[0,1]\), consider the following property: there exists a finite graph \(H_c\) containing no cycle of length \(3\) such that, for every integer \(n\geq1\), every graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices containing no cycle of length \(3\) or \(5\), and in which every vertex has at least \(cn\) neighbors, admits a homomorphism to \(H_c\). The graph \(H_c\) may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n\) or \(G\).

What is the exact infimum of the numbers \(c\in[0,1]\) having this property?

\[
\boxed{\frac15}

The relevant result is the **sharp odd-girth homomorphism-threshold theorem**. Its \(7\)-odd-girth case has the following two parts:

* For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a finite graph \(F_\varepsilon\) of odd girth at least \(7\) such that every graph \(G\) of odd girth at least \(7\) with
  \[
  \delta(G)\ge \left(\frac15+\varepsilon\right)|V(G)|
  \]
  admits a homomorphism to \(F_\varepsilon\).
* For every \(\varepsilon>0\) and every finite triangle-free graph \(H\), there is a graph \(G\) of odd girth at least \(7\) such that
  \[
  \delta(G)\ge \left(\frac15-\varepsilon\right)|V(G)|
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad G\nrightarrow H.
  \]
  Importantly, this lower-bound statement allows the proposed target \(H\) to contain \(5\)-cycles.

Here, having odd girth at least \(7\) is exactly the condition of containing neither a \(3\)-cycle nor a \(5\)-cycle.

If \(c>1/5\), apply the first part with \(\varepsilon=c-1/5\). The resulting \(F_\varepsilon\) is, in particular, triangle-free, so it can serve as \(H_c\).

Conversely, let \(c<1/5\) and suppose a finite triangle-free target \(H_c\) existed. Choose \(\varepsilon>0\) with \(1/5-\varepsilon>c\). The second part gives a graph satisfying all the hypotheses in the question, with minimum degree greater than \(c|V(G)|\), but with no homomorphism to \(H_c\), a contradiction.

Thus every \(c>1/5\) works and every \(c<1/5\) fails. Whether the endpoint itself works is unnecessary for determining the infimum.

My previous answer incorrectly strengthened a lower-bound theorem: an obstruction to bounded targets of **odd girth at least \(7\)** need not obstruct bounded **triangle-free** targets.

The relevant bounded-target theorem is:

> For every \(\eta>0\), there is an integer \(M(\eta)\) such that every graph \(G\) containing neither a triangle nor a pentagon and satisfying
> \[
> \delta(G)\ge \eta |V(G)|
> \]
> admits a homomorphism to a triangle-free graph with at most \(M(\eta)\) vertices.

The target in this theorem is allowed to contain pentagons. To obtain the single target required in the question, take the disjoint union of one representative of every triangle-free graph on at most \(M(\eta)\) vertices. This is a finite triangle-free graph, and every \(G\) covered by the theorem maps to it. Consequently, **every \(c>0\) has the required property**, proving that the infimum is zero.

\[
A_r=K_{(5r+2)/(2r+1)}.
\]
They contain neither triangles nor pentagons and have minimum-degree proportion
\[
\frac{r+1}{5r+2}\longrightarrow\frac15.
\]

\[
f(i)=\left\lfloor\frac{5i}{5r+2}\right\rfloor
\]
is a homomorphism. Thus these graphs cannot supply the claimed lower bound when pentagons are permitted in the target.

content.text:
My claim that the infimum is zero was wrong. A concrete construction gives a positive lower bound—and distinguishes unbounded homomorphic complexity from unbounded chromatic number.

Here is a rigorous lower bound of \(1/9\).

Let
\[
Q=KG(m,k),
\]
whose vertices are the \(k\)-subsets of \([m]\), with disjointness defining adjacency. Choose \(m=2k+s\), where \(s\to\infty\) but \(s/k\to0\). Then
\[
\chi(Q)=s+2\longrightarrow\infty.
\]

Orient the edges of \(Q\) arbitrarily and replace each oriented edge \(uv\) by
\[
u-a_{uv}-b_{uv}-v.
\]
Call the resulting graph \(F\). Give its vertices three types and set-labels:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{vertex}&\text{type}&\text{label}\\ \hline
u&0&u\\
a_{uv}&1&u\\
b_{uv}&2&v.
\end{array}
\]
A useful observation is that endpoints of any length-three walk in \(F\) having the same type have disjoint labels.

For each type \(t\) and index \(i\in[m]\), introduce an independent set \(A_{t,i}\) of size \(T\). Join a vertex of \(F\) to all of \(A_{t,i}\) precisely when it has type \(t\) and its label contains \(i\). Finally, for each type introduce an independent set \(B_t\) of size \(kT\), complete to all the sets \(A_{t,i}\) of that type. Add no other edges.

The resulting graph \(G\) has no triangle or pentagon:

* Each type class of \(F\) is independent.
* A pentagon using exactly one auxiliary vertex would require a length-three walk between same-type vertices with intersecting labels.
* Pentagons involving more auxiliary vertices are excluded by the three separate bipartite auxiliary components.

Moreover,
\[
|V(G)|=|V(F)|+3(m+k)T,
\qquad
\delta(G)\ge kT.
\]
Taking \(T\) large and then \(m/k\to2\) makes the minimum-degree proportion approach \(1/9\).

Yet these graphs cannot all map to a fixed finite triangle-free graph \(H\). Indeed, such a homomorphism would map every subdivided edge of \(Q\) to a length-three walk in \(H\). The graph on \(V(H)\) joining endpoints of length-three walks is loopless, because \(H\) is triangle-free. Consequently,
\[
\chi(Q)\le |V(H)|,
\]
contradicting \(\chi(Q)\to\infty\).

Thus the requested infimum is **at least \(1/9\)**. The standard bounded-target theorem for odd-girth-seven graphs gives the upper bound \(1/5\), so the conclusions I can substantiate are
\[
\boxed{\frac19\le \inf c\le\frac15}.
\]

I have not established the exact value. In particular, neither my earlier answer \(0\) nor my unsupported strengthening of the lower-bound theorem to obtain \(1/5\) should be treated as a valid solution.
